subskill: Counting integer solutions inside a range that depends on k
prompt:
-53 ≤ 10 - 3x < -17
For how many positive integer values of k are at least one-third of the positive integers less than or equal to k solutions to the compound inequality above?
explanation: First solve the compound inequality. Subtracting 10 gives -63 ≤ -3x < -27, and dividing by -3 reverses both signs: 21 ≥ x > 9. So the solutions are the integers 10, 11, ..., 21 - twelve of them. Note which ends are attained: x = 21 IS a solution (it came from the ≤), and x = 9 is NOT (it came from the <). Now let c be the number of solutions among 1, 2, ..., k; the condition is c ≥ k/3, that is, 3c ≥ k. If k ≤ 9, c = 0, so the condition fails. If 10 ≤ k ≤ 21, c = k - 9, and 3(k - 9) ≥ k gives k ≥ 13.5, so k = 14, ..., 21: 8 values. If k ≥ 21, all twelve solutions are counted, c = 12, and 36 ≥ k gives k = 22, ..., 36 (k = 21 is already counted): 15 values. Total: 8 + 15 = 23. Choice 25 comes from reversing the signs but leaving the 'or equal' at its original end, which makes the solutions 9 through 20. Choice 22 reads 'at least one-third' as 'more than one-third', which loses k = 36. Choice 16 counts only the values of k for which all twelve solutions are already among 1 through k (k = 21 to 36) and misses the smaller values of k.
solve: const P=x=>{const m=10-3*x; return -53<=m && m< -17}; let n=0; for (let k=1;k<=500;k++){ let c=0; for (let x=1;x<=k;x++) if (P(x)) c++; if (3*c>=k) n++; } return n;

mechanism: reverse a compound inequality and keep track of the attained end
count of solutions up to k is piecewise (k - 9, then 12)
quantity_asked: the number of positive integers k for which at least one-third of the integers 1 through k satisfy the compound inequality

setup.i: k is the upper end of the range of positive integers tested; the compound inequality (negative x-coefficient) has no constant
setup.ii: at least one-third of the positive integers up to k are solutions
setup.iii: number of positive integer values of k

plugback.why: The ask is how many k work. A candidate count like 23 cannot be put into the inequality or the one-third condition; checking it requires finding the whole set of k (both pieces), which is the full solution. The key is at try 3 in ascending order in any case.

25.why: Leaving the 'or equal' where it was when the signs reverse shifts the solution block down by one (9 to 20 instead of 10 to 21). That makes the first piece start earlier but also keeps the block at twelve integers, so the net effect is not visible from the stem; here it gives two extra k.

22.why: Treating 'at least' as 'more than' drops the equality case; the stem gives no way to tell whether equality is ever reached (it is, at k = 36 only), so the side is not signalled.

16.why: Counting only the k past the last solution drops the first piece; nothing in the stem says a second piece exists, so the student cannot see 16 is short.
